canonical_definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats harmlessness as a latent model tendency or response quality defined by not generating harmful, unsafe, unethical, offensive, or toxic content, often even under harmful or adversarial prompts. Many papers make this concrete with examples such as illegal advice, discrimination, misinformation, self-harm, violence, or other socially damaging outputs, and some connect it to refusing harmful requests. A smaller line narrows the setting to particular contexts, including malicious multimodal inputs, advice-seeking, hallucinations in critical applications, or eating-disorder-related content, so definitions differ mainly on model-level disposition versus output-level quality, and on broad safety harms versus task-specific harms.

Space of facets. Most papers place harmlessness beside helpfulness and honesty as one of the recurring 3H or HHH alignment objectives, and some extend this multi-objective framing with humor. Several evaluation setups split data into helpful and harmless subsets, while one advice-focused line treats harmlessness as an evaluation axis independent of helpfulness. A smaller line uses neighboring labels such as harmfulness or safety, and an auditing paper explicitly says harmlessness "encompasses a range of considerations" and is interpreted and operationalized by crowdworkers.

Space of measurement. Papers link harmlessness to 33 measurement instruments and 5 behavioral indicators. The most common operationalizations use HH-RLHF, LLM-as-a-judge, PKU-SafeRLHF, Human evaluation, and AdvBench: preference datasets ask which response is more helpful and harmless or mark whether a preferred response meets safety standards, LLM judges often score pairs on harmlessness together with helpfulness, relevance, accuracy, and insightfulness, human raters compare outputs for harmlessness, and adversarial benchmarks test behavior on harmful or jailbreak prompts. Many other instruments also appear, including other harmful-query benchmarks, safety classifiers, moderation or toxicity APIs, and agent-focused evaluations, so most measures match the dominant safety framing, though a smaller set operationalizes it through toxicity tools or other task benchmarks.

Links. The most recurring link is to Helpfulness: many papers say harmlessness is related to helpfulness, often as a tension, trade-off, or competing objective, and several report that it correlates negatively with helpfulness. Harmlessness is also related to Human preference alignment, papers claim a causal relationship from Safety alignment to harmlessness, other papers separately report that harmlessness correlates with or is related to Safety alignment, papers claim a causal relationship from Alignment to harmlessness, and some papers relate it to or report correlations with Humor. Overall, harmlessness is linked to 9 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators, with the remaining links mostly connecting it to refusal-oriented or harmful-output behaviors, including single-paper causal claims from other traits to harmlessness and from harmlessness to one output behavior.

characterization_sections.label: Space of definitions.
characterization_sections.text: Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats harmlessness as a latent model tendency or response quality defined by not generating harmful, unsafe, unethical, offensive, or toxic content, often even under harmful or adversarial prompts. Many papers make this concrete with examples such as illegal advice, discrimination, misinformation, self-harm, violence, or other socially damaging outputs, and some connect it to refusing harmful requests. A smaller line narrows the setting to particular contexts, including malicious multimodal inputs, advice-seeking, hallucinations in critical applications, or eating-disorder-related content, so definitions differ mainly on model-level disposition versus output-level quality, and on broad safety harms versus task-specific harms.

characterization_sections.label: Space of facets.
characterization_sections.text: Most papers place harmlessness beside helpfulness and honesty as one of the recurring 3H or HHH alignment objectives, and some extend this multi-objective framing with humor. Several evaluation setups split data into helpful and harmless subsets, while one advice-focused line treats harmlessness as an evaluation axis independent of helpfulness. A smaller line uses neighboring labels such as harmfulness or safety, and an auditing paper explicitly says harmlessness "encompasses a range of considerations" and is interpreted and operationalized by crowdworkers.

characterization_sections.label: Space of measurement.
characterization_sections.text: Papers link harmlessness to 33 measurement instruments and 5 behavioral indicators. The most common operationalizations use HH-RLHF, LLM-as-a-judge, PKU-SafeRLHF, Human evaluation, and AdvBench: preference datasets ask which response is more helpful and harmless or mark whether a preferred response meets safety standards, LLM judges often score pairs on harmlessness together with helpfulness, relevance, accuracy, and insightfulness, human raters compare outputs for harmlessness, and adversarial benchmarks test behavior on harmful or jailbreak prompts. Many other instruments also appear, including other harmful-query benchmarks, safety classifiers, moderation or toxicity APIs, and agent-focused evaluations, so most measures match the dominant safety framing, though a smaller set operationalizes it through toxicity tools or other task benchmarks.

characterization_sections.label: Links.
characterization_sections.text: The most recurring link is to Helpfulness: many papers say harmlessness is related to helpfulness, often as a tension, trade-off, or competing objective, and several report that it correlates negatively with helpfulness. Harmlessness is also related to Human preference alignment, papers claim a causal relationship from Safety alignment to harmlessness, other papers separately report that harmlessness correlates with or is related to Safety alignment, papers claim a causal relationship from Alignment to harmlessness, and some papers relate it to or report correlations with Humor. Overall, harmlessness is linked to 9 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators, with the remaining links mostly connecting it to refusal-oriented or harmful-output behaviors, including single-paper causal claims from other traits to harmlessness and from harmlessness to one output behavior.

definition_agreement.reason: Most papers define harmlessness as a model or response-level tendency to avoid producing harmful, unsafe, unethical, toxic, or dangerous content, often including refusal under adversarial or malicious prompts. A few papers narrow this to particular harms or phrase it as the inverse risk of generating harmful content, but they still target the same core property rather than a different phenomenon.
